In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning. We demonstrate that using a single learned dynamics model
for multiple tasks doesn't always result in desirable outcomes; in some cases,
it can lead to significant performance degradation. To overcome this challenge, we
propose two innovative approaches: one uses separate sub-networks for each task
and conditions them on overlapping experience to minimize knowledge loss;
another employs a more centralized architecture where a global model is trained
on a combined dataset of all tasks. We validate these approaches on a variety
of multi-task environments and find that they achieve comparable performance to
non-shared learning controls. Moreover, we observe that many existing multi-task
RL datasets align with our setup and could be used with modified versions of
our methods.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article provides a detailed explanation for the lack of invariant planes in systems governed by a fractional differential equation of higher order. A key aspect of dynamical systems, invariant subspaces play a significant role in studying and solving differential equations by splitting them into smaller, more manageable components. However, our research indicates that for systems beyond a certain order, there are no invariant subspaces available, despite satisfying a crucial stability condition. This discovery is particularly notable for higher order differential systems, where the absence of invariant subspaces can significantly impact the system's behavior and solutions. 

In particular, we offer a specific example involving a second-order differential system in three dimensions, for which no invariant planes exist despite the system's stable and conservative nature. This example can be generalized to higher dimensional spaces, offering new insights into the behavior of these complex systems. 

One interesting connection worth noting is between the lack of invariant planes in these systems and the conservation laws that these systems adhere to. While our findings indicate that the combination of a system being both conservative and higher order results in the absence of invariant planes, the opposite holds true for lower order systems - they either have or lack specific conservation laws, respectively. 

The article also addresses a previously reported error in the research published by Cauli and co-authors, due to an overextension of a particular assumption made in their study. 

Our research into these complex systems can be found in sections 2 through 5 of the article, with section 6 offering some concluding remarks

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the purely data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long-term periodic signal patterns and short-term signal fragments. Experimental evaluations under both unconditional and text-to-speech synthesis settings demonstrate the improved pitch control and higher quality generation of QPNet in comparison to WaveNet and PDCNN architectures.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), Picard gauging, and stable homotopy, in addition to Axelson-Hopkins' trace conjectures. Through the integration of Berman-Lin's results on THH with respect to functors that preserve monoids, the concept of shadows is rigorously defined within the realm of bicategorical functors. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the composite of a functor that forms shadows and a functor that generates traces results in a bicategorical extension of Runkers' trace conjecture, providing a precise and formal expression.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN leverages a neighbourhood aggregation approach and introduces a new operation called Lorentzian graph convolution, and through extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets, it demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, given incomplete information in the form of sensor data from the acoustic system. The data represents incomplete information about the system's solution at a specific time interval. Using a control theory approach, we establish a regularized method to approximate the source term by minimizing a functional that represents the discrepancy between the calculated solution and the available sensor data, combined with a penalty term to limit the source term's variation. A convergence analysis is provided, and the effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical experiments.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both employed to analyze the complex thermal equilibrium states.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. A detailed analysis of the simplest scoto-seesaw model reveals that it meets all current theoretical and experimental standards. Furthermore, we find that the dark sector's impact on neutrino scales contributes to a positive impact on the Higgs field's stability in the high-temperature limit. Moreover, we establish that the model naturally accommodates the dark matter abundance observed in the cosmos with minimal additional constraints. When compared to leading dark matter candidates, we find that the model's characteristic 75 GeV resonance results in distinct relic abundance patterns. Consequently, this indicates that the model can be distinguished from leading dark matter candidates through LHC experiments that search for high-energy resonance signatures.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the impact of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of these localized $d$-electrons in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. The study indicates that in both 4d and 5d materials, the magnitude of orbital occupation remains near 0.5 when spin-orbit coupling is substantial, and the degree of magnetic moment varies significantly with electron filling, presenting two distinct configurations: a low-electron-fillings situation with the magnetic moment close to 1.5 $\mu_B$, and a high-electron-fillings scenario with the magnetic moment near 2 $\mu_B$. The study also reveals that the band widths associated with $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ are equivalent, and the material can be theoretically considered as a low or high-electron-fillings case, with the transition occurring with the filling of three electrons per orbital. The theoretical predictions are compared with available experimental data for 4d and 5d transition metal oxides.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated by modifying a pre-trained model to correct artificial distortions added to real chest X-rays with the goal of retraining it to distinguish normal X-rays from various disease classes, using 14 classes defined in the CheXpert dataset. These classes encompass both minor and severe conditions, including atelectasis, cardiomegaly, and pneumothorax. A comparison with a more complex medical GAN model, medGAN, shows our simple approach yields comparable results for 12 classes and surpasses it in 2 classes, utilizing a significantly smaller dataset of distorted X-rays with an order of magnitude difference in model complexity. To validate our approach for modeling multi-class diseases, we utilized a leave-one-out cross-validation strategy and achieved an accuracy of 73.3% in identifying normal X-rays and 55.3% in distinguishing between different disease classes. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/krishnaair/CCGAN.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
